DISCUSSION

There was great temporal and spatial (depth and geography) variability in our field measurements of N₂ fixation in the Baltic Sea. The apparent patchiness and temporal fluctuations in cyanobacterial abundance and rates of N₂ fixation confirm the importance of long-term inter-annual studies over a wide arrary of sampling stations for obtaining comprehensive information required for decisions on sewage treatment and nutrient management efforts.

Diel variability and calculations of N₂ fixation in filamentous cyanobacteria

In filamentous cyanobacteria such as Aphanizomenon, Nodularia and Anabaena, the oxygen-sensitive enzyme nitrogenase is protected by heterocysts allowing maximal rates of N₂ fixation during daytime photo-

</page>

<page number="7">

synthesis. This diel pattern in N_2 fixation (Fig. 2B) has been reported in several investigations of heterocystous cyanobacteria from the Baltic Sea (Brattberg 1977, Vuorio et al. 1978, Evans et al. 2000, Gallon et al. 2002). A number of diel estimates of N_2 fixation in the Baltic Sea are based on short, daytime measurements. Brattberg (1977), however, found that the average rate of N_2 fixation between 10:00 and 14:00 h comprised only 28% of the total 24 h rate, which is close to our area integration of AR during the same daytime period (34%; Fig. 2A). According to the pre-filtered \(^{15}\)N incubations, mean nocturnal N_2 fixation rates were 13 and 25% of the average daytime fixation rates at Stns B1 and BY31, respectively (Table 1). In our diel measurements, total integrated N_2 fixation at night was 20% of total daytime fixation (06:00 to 20:00 integration, Fig. 2A). This is slightly lower than the range (23 to 50%) reported for *Aphanizomenon* colonies (Horne 1979, Storch et al. 1990, Evans et al. 2000, Gallon et al. 2002), but similar to 20% reported by Vuorio et al. (1978). Therefore, diazotrophic activities during the dark period may also contribute significantly to the total rate of N_2 fixation in aquatic environments and should not be overlooked in diel estimates. In this study we propose a way to extrapolate diel rates of N_2 fixation using measurements of short-term N_2 fixation and the daily surface irradiance curve (see equation in Results). The calculated diel rate of N_2 fixation appeared to follow actual 24 h rates measured coincidentally at Stn BY31 (Fig. 2B).

DON utilization and N_2 fixation in non-filamentous cyanobacteria

Passive leakage or active release of DON has frequently been documented in actively growing phytoplankton (Bronk et al. 1994, Glibert & Bronk 1994, Mulholland et al. 2004). However, whether or not healthy growing cells excrete DON is still under debate (Bronk & Ward 2000, Slawyk et al. 1998). Reported rates of DON release from cyanobacteria are in the range of 40 to 50% of the rate of N_2 fixation (Glibert & Bronk 1994), but the rate of excretion may depend on physiological growth conditions. The molar ratio between AR and \(^{15}\)N_2 incorporation varied in Baltic Sea cyanobacteria during the course of a diel cycle (Gallon et al. 2002). Therefore, the \(^{15}\)N-enrichment method may not have reflected gross N_2 fixation as release of \(^{15}\)N-labelled DON may have caused the high molar ratios observed in their study (Gallon et al. 2002). We are aware of no specific studies of DON excretion from Baltic Sea diazotrophic cyanobacteria. No detectable rates of N_2 fixation in cells <5 \( \mu \)m were observed during daytime in offshore waters of the Baltic Sea, but 5 to 10% of the total N_2 fixed was recovered in these cells and attributed to DON transfer from the larger filamentous cyanobacteria to the 'picoplankton' fraction (Ohlendieck et al. 2000). Of total N_2 fixation 43% occurred in cyanobacterial cells <10 \( \mu \)m (Wasmund et al. 2001). This size fraction, however, had the same level of \(^{15}\)N-enrichment in pre-screened cells and cells separated after the incubations, suggesting that DON excretion was insignificant for cells <10 \( \mu \)m in their study. Higher night-time rates in natural seawater samples (up to 1.9 \( \times \) the daytime rate) suggested that smaller non-filamentous diazotrophs may have been more active at night (Wasmund et al. 2001). Recent open ocean studies using the \(^{15}\)N method have demonstrated the significance of night-time N_2 fixation by single cell diazotrophs (Montoya et al. 2004). At times, significant rates of N_2 fixation have also been found in cells other than filamentous cyanobacteria (Wasmund et al. 2001), and a variable but significant fraction of N_2 fixation has been observed in cells between 5 \( \mu \)m and 20 \( \mu \)m (Ohlendieck et al. 2007). Therefore, assuming that cells <5 \( \mu \)m are non-diazotrophic and incorporate excreted DON, we can deduce that cells between 5 \( \mu \)m and 10 \( \mu \)m may sometimes contribute significantly to N_2 fixation in the water column. In our study, most N_2 fixation occurred in cells >20 \( \mu \)m (Fig. 3). However, a considerable fraction of the \(^{15}\)N-label in our diel incubations (31 to 44% of total N_2 fixation at H4, 15 to 24% at X1, and 18 to 28% at BY31) was also recovered in cells <20 \( \mu \)m. In a day-night comparison of N_2 fixation with size-fractionated samples, the coastal stations had higher rates in the smaller cell fraction in daytime rather than at night (Table 1). Only at Stn BY31 did cells <20 \( \mu \)m have higher rates of N_2 fixation at night than during the day. Our data suggest that non-filamentous cyanobacteria in offshore waters may at times have significant rates of N_2 fixation at night. However, the average fractions of \(^{15}\)N enrichment in cells <20 \( \mu \)m in this study (Fig. 3) far exceeded the rates of N_2 fixation attributed to non-filamentous cyanobacteria in the Baltic Sea (Ohlendieck et al. 2007). Therefore, we conclude that a significant proportion of the total N_2 fixation was initially incorporated by filamentous cyanobacteria and, by way of DON excretion, may have been further assimilated by microplankton.

Cyanobacterial blooms and growth

The great variability in the abundance of filamentous cyanobacteria and hence, their potential contribution to new production by N_2 fixation may result from a multitude of physical, chemical and physiological factors. Previous studies (see overview by Leppänen et al. 1988) reported a relationship between rates of N_2 fixation, surface temperature and the stability of the water

</page>

<page number="8">

column. Although SST and the water column stability index may appear to be important correlates of bloom formation in filamentous cyanobacteria, we did not see any direct relationship between these factors and increased cell abundance and elevated rates of N₂ fixation (Figs. 4 to 6). However, surface stability in offshore waters (Stn BY31) reverted to winter levels in the time preceding the expected bloom of cyanobacteria in the summers of 1998 and 2000, and this may explain, in part, the low rates of N₂ fixation measured in these 2 years (Fig. 4). The surface water stability index also had intermittent lapses in early summer of 1999 at Stn BY31 when cell abundance and N₂ fixation rates were high, but the lapses were less frequent and not as severe as in the other years. Surface water stability was stronger in inshore waters, and Stn X1 had a relatively high stability index through the summer of 2000, coincident with the highest abundance of filamentous cyanobacteria and rates of N₂ fixation during the 3 yr study (Fig. 5). This pattern was not as apparent at the innermost Stn H4, where water column stability was often higher than at the other stations investigated (Fig. 6). In fact, an extended period of high surface temperatures followed by high water column stability prevailed in the summer of 1999 at Stn H4 and yet, these conditions did not generate any increase in the abundance of filamentous cyanobacteria, and the rates of N₂ fixation were the lowest recorded within the study period (Fig. 6).

Relatively high dissolved N:P nutrient ratios in the inner parts of the bay may have favoured the growth of non-diazotroph phytoplankton with higher affinity for P, a circumstance previously suggested by Wallström (1988). We therefore conclude that dissolved nutrient concentrations with a low N:P ratio are important in determining the presence and extent of N₂ fixing cyanobacteria in surface waters, as suggested by Smith (1983). Moreover, the generally high N:P ratios in Bothnian Bay have been used to explain the absence of filamentous cyanobacteria in that region of the Baltic Sea (Niemi 1979, Rinne et al. 1981). In addition to a low dissolved N:P ratio, high concentrations of P may also promote and sustain blooms of cyanobacteria (Wallström et al. 1992, Wasmund 1997). High levels of available phosphate stimulate growth and rates of N₂ fixation in cyanobacteria collected from natural populations (Horstmann 1975, Kononen et al. 1998, Moisander et al. 2003), in mesocosms (Wallström et al. 1992) and in laboratory cultures (Huber 1986, Moisander & Paerl 2000). In contrast, high ambient concentrations of combined dissolved nitrogen can cause a reduction in N₂ fixation (Huber 1986). Therefore, the high rates of N₂ fixation measured at Stns H4 and X1 in the summer of 2000 (Figs. 5A, 6A) may, in part, have been stimulated by the higher concentrations of phosphate (0.05 to 0.15 μM) in the Himmerfjärden bay area during that particular year (U. Larsson pers. comm.). Our results demonstrate the multitude of parameters that may affect cyanobacterial growth and N₂ fixation.

Balanced growth of cyanobacteria (i.e. cellular C:N:P ratios approximating the Redfield relationship of 106:16:1, Redfield et al. 1963) requires a flux of dissolved N and P in a ratio that is constant to that of photosynthetically derived C (Dubinsky & Berman-Frank 2001). Our particle fractionation technique did not discriminate detrital matter from live cells. Therefore, the presence of detritus (with extremely high C:N and C:P) in particles >20 μm may have overestimated these ratios. The C:N ratios in cells >20 μm (the fraction largely dominated by filamentous cyanobacteria) were slightly higher or grouped around the Redfield relationship of 6.6 (Figs. 4 to 6) and similar to the mass ratios for Aphanizomenon and Nodularia in the same area (Larsson et al. 2001, Walve 2002). The high molar C:P ratios in particles >20 μm at Stn BY31 in summer were also similar but slightly higher than those reported by others (Larsson et al. 2001, Walve 2002) using more refined techniques to separate filamentous cyanobacteria. The high C:P ratios found in filamentous cyanobacteria in offshore waters indicated severe P-limitation in the diazotrophs in summer (Larsson et al. 2001). While C:P in the fraction >20 μm remained similar in 1998 and 1999 at Stn BY31, the elemental mass ratio increased dramatically between the years at Stns X1 and H4 (Figs. 5B, 6B). This observation, combined with the molar C:N ratio at Stns X1 and H4, suggests that cells >20 μm were initially P-replete and may have transformed into an N-replete community during summer by the end of our field study. The N-replete community >20 μm may have been supported by the high rates of N₂ fixation (relative to previous years) in the summer of 2000 at Stns X1 and H4 (Figs. 5A, 6A).

Spatial variability in rates of N₂ fixation

Highest rates of N₂ fixation were found in surface waters (Fig. 3), in good agreement with earlier studies from the Baltic Sea (Brattberg 1977, Vuorio et al. 1978, Niemistö et al. 1989, Evans et al. 2000, Wasmund et al. 2001, Gallon et al. 2002). The low rates of N₂ fixation measured at 20 m depth (Fig. 3) can be attributed to low biomass of heterocystous cyanobacteria and low light at these depths (Stal & Walsby 1998, Wasmund et al. 2001). Vertical biomass distribution in the open Baltic Sea shows that maximum abundance of Aphanizomenon is frequently around 10 m depth, while Nodularia aggregates in surface waters (Walsby et al.

</page>

<page number="9">
1995, Heiskanen & Olli 1996, Wasmund et al. 2001, Hajdu et al. 2007). Therefore, a significant and active part of the diazotrophic community may exist in subsurface waters and must be included in order to obtain accurate estimates of total water column N_2 fixation rates (Stal & Walsby 1998).

Cyanobacterial biomass had abrupt seasonal maxima and great inter-annual differences at our stations (Figs. 4B, 5B, 6B). Although Aphanizomenon sp. was most frequent, surface blooms of Nodularia sp. often occurred during summer at the offshore Stn BY31. An overview of the abundance distribution of filamentous cyanobacteria in the Baltic Sea (Finni et al. 2001) also shows that Aphanizomenon sp. is the most commonly encountered species in recent history. The positive linear relationship between average abundance of filamentous cyanobacteria and the rate of N_2 fixation (Fig. 7) largely explains the rather ephemeral biomass distribution and the temporal and spatial variability in measured rates of total N_2 fixation.

We calculated annual depth-integrated estimates of N_2 fixation for each of our stations (Table 2). Missing months in some of the years were extrapolated from the adjacent months or by using averages from other years in which measurements were made. There was considerable variability in the annual rates of N_2 fixation at the coastal Stns H4, X1 and the offshore Stn BY31, but these differences appeared to even out in the 3 yr averages of total N_2 fixation (calculated from Table 2: 400 and 545 mgN m^{-2} yr^{-1} for Stns H4 and X1, respectively, and 555 mgN m^{-2} yr^{-1} for Stn BY31). The annual averages of N_2 fixation in cells >20 μm at the coastal stations (21 and 31 mmol N m^{-2}) also fell within the annual range (21 to 78 mmol N m^{-2}) reported by Lindahl et al. (1978). At offshore Stn BY31, our total annual estimates for 1998–2000 (range 22 to 51 mmol N m^{-2}) were similar to the rates measured at coastal Stns X1 and H4. Coastal waters are frequently ignored in annual estimates of N_2 fixation to the Baltic Sea. We suggest that diazotrophic cyanobacteria may contribute significantly to new primary production in both coastal and open waters of the Baltic Sea.

Significance of N_2 fixation in the Baltic Sea

The annual contribution of N_2 fixation to new N in the Baltic Proper was estimated from depth integrated (0 to 10 m) diel rates of N_2 fixation from the offshore Stn BY31. Assuming that 240 000 km^2 is a representative area of the Baltic Proper (Rolff et al. 2007), we calculated an annual input of fixed nitrogen to new production in the order of 56 000 to 125 000 t (Table 3). This estimate is within the range of some of the earlier studies (Rinne et al. 1978, Brattberg 1980, Niemistö et al. 1989, Hübel & Hübel 1995, Rahm et al. 2000), but significantly lower than most recent studies (Larsson et al. 2001, Wasmund et al. 2001, 2005, Rolff et al. 2007). In a recent study, Rolff et al. (2007) showed that the abundance of Aphanizomenon (one of the major contributors to N_2 fixation) was higher and lasted longer through the summer at all stations south of Stn BY31 in the Baltic Sea. Therefore, annual integrated rates of N_2 fixation extrapolated from regions south of BY31 might generate higher estimates than ours. Indeed, the more recent estimates of N_2 fixation (Larsson et al. 2001, Wasmund et al. 2001, 2005, Rolff et al. 2007) were all generated from locations south and east of Stn BY31 (Table 3). This observation emphasizes the need for a sampling strategy with high spatial diversity and high temporal frequency in biogeochemical studies of the Baltic Sea (Ohlendieck et al. 2007, Rolff et al. 2007). The annual input of \( N_2 \) fixation to the Himmerfjärden Bay area alone (179 km\(^2\); Stns H4 and X1) was very variable and the estimates should be regarded with caution. Therefore, we are only considering here the 3 yr annual averages of 65 t N at Stn H4 and 89 t N at Stn X1 (calculated from Table 2). The estimated annual discharge of N from the sewage treatment plant in the Himmerfjärden bay area (Fig. 1) was on average 130 t N during the period of our study (Elmgren & Larsson 2001). This is in sharp contrast to previous years (1976–1994) when the annual load ranged between 500 and 900 t N (Elmgren & Larsson 2001). Due to legislation, the sewage treatment plant today removes 90% of the annual load of total N. Prior to 1998, the sewage treatment plant was a significant point source contributing on average 40% of the annual input of total N to the bay area. Our estimates suggest that during the study period the reduction in N discharged from the sewage treatment plant was not compensated for by an increase in new N via cyanobacterial \( N_2 \) fixation. After agricultural run-off and sewage discharge, \( N_2 \) fixation was still only the third largest source of new N to the Himmerfjärden bay area. However, the large annual variability in the measured rates of \( N_2 \) fixation in the bay area demonstrates the need to investigate the multitude of factors determining cyanobacterial growth and \( N_2 \) fixation. This effort should be considered before costly nutrient waste management efforts are implemented.

Clough Below-ground nitrogen cycling in relation to net canopy production in mangrove forests of southern Thailand Received: 14 June 2001 / Accepted: 1 November 2001 / Published online: 18 January 2002 © Springer-Verlag 2002 Abstract Rates of accumulation, transformation and availability of sediment nitrogen in four mangrove forests of different age and type in southern Thailand were examined in relation to forest net canopy production. Net ammonification (range: 0.3–2.3 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)), nitrification (range: 0–0.7 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) and nitrogen fixation (range: 0–0.6 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) in surface sediments equated to <10% of canopy nitrogen demand (range: 7.5–32 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)). By mass balance, we estimated that most of the nitrogen required for tree growth must be derived from root-associated nitrogen fixation and/or mineralisation processes occurring possibly to the maximum depth of live root penetration (75–100 cm). Denitrification, nitrification, rainfall and tidal exchange were comparatively small components of sediment nitrogen flow. Denitrification (range: 0–3.8 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) removed 3–6% of total nitrogen input at three Rhizophora forests, but removed 23% of total nitrogen input in a high-intertidal Ceriops forest. Nitrogen burial ranged from 4% to 12% of total nitrogen input, with the greatest burial rates in two forests receiving the least tidal inundation. Inputs of nitrogen to the forests were rapid (range: 11–37 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)), likely originating from upstream sources such as agricultural and industrial lands, sewage and shrimp ponds. Our results indicate that ~70% to 90% of the nitrogen supplied to the forest floor is shunted via the ammonium pool to trees to sustain the rapid rates of net canopy production measured in these forests. Differences in plant–sediment nitrogen relations between the forests appeared to be a function of the interaction between intertidal position and stand age. Introduction Most mangrove forests are either nitrogen or phosphorus limited (Alongi 1998). Fertilisation experiments (Boto and Wellington 1983; Boto et al. 1985), and the fact that mangroves appear to be highly efficient in retaining and recycling nutrients (Nedwell et al. 1994; Kristensen et al. 1995), support the notion of nutrient limitation. The pathways of nutrient cycling in mangrove forests are poorly understood. Nutrient availability and use are thought to depend upon several interrelated factors: the sources and composition of labile organic matter, inorganic nutrient pools, frequency of tidal flooding, temperature, salinity, soil chemistry, tree physiology and solar radiation (Ball 1988; Alongi 1998). For instance, a large fraction of interstitial ammonium is bound to soil particles and exchangeable with other cations. The kinetics of ion exchange between the free and exchangeable ammonium pools in saline soils is, however, very complex and dynamic. The availability of nitrogen in forms capable of being readily assimilated by mangroves is a microbial controlled process, with the bacterial breakdown of organic nitrogen as the major rate-limiting step. Knowledge of nitrogen transformation in mangrove sediments is limited. Individual processes such as denitrification and nitrogen fixation have been measured in a number of mangrove forests (Nedwell et al. 1994; Rivera-Monroy and Twilley 1996; Kristensen et al. 1998). Ammonification has been measured, but most methods cannot distinguish gross and net (after biological uptake) production rates. How these specific transformation processes relate to one another, and to the deposition rate of organic matter and to tree requirements, has been demonstrated only in Rhizophora forests in northern Australia (Alongi 1998) and in south-western Thailand (Kristensen et al. 1998, 2000). In both of these forests, rates of nitrogen transformation are slow compared to other estuarine ecosystems, with some indication that inorganic nitrogen not assimilated by the trees and other autotrophs is immobilised within the sediment. How the rate of nitrogen flow relates to canopy production and the rate of nitrogen deposition is unknown. To understand these processes, it is necessary to measure the rate and efficiency of nutrient cycling in relation to stand age and net primary production. Data from terrestrial forests indicate that as forests age, net primary production declines, as does nutrient flow (Gower et al. 1996). There is some evidence that mangrove primary production decreases with stand age, but the reasons are unclear (Clough et al. 2000a,b). In the current paper, we present empirical data on the rate of accumulation, transformation and availability of sediment nitrogen pools in one mature (~25 years old) forest and three young (3–5 years old) mangrove forests located in Sawi Bay in southern Thailand. We use this data with previously published data on rates of net canopy production and sediment mass accumulation to construct preliminary nitrogen budgets. Materials and methods Study sites Four mangrove forests were sampled during the dry north-east monsoon (April 1999) and during the wet south-west monsoon (October 1999) in Sawi Bay (Ao Sawi), located on the south-western coast of the Gulf of Thailand (Fig. 1). The climate of southern Thailand is dominated by the two monsoon seasons (Nieuwolt 1981). Water temperatures vary within a narrow range of 27–30°C; rainfall is much greater in the wet season (8–34 mm day\(^{-1}\)) than in the dry season (0–3 mm day\(^{-1}\)), with an annual average of 1,800 mm (Wattayakorn et al. 2000). Sawi Bay has mixed semi-diurnal tides, with a tidal range of 1.5 m (Wattayakorn et al. 2000). Sawi Bay has experienced dramatic changes in land use and mangrove clearing, to the extent that a forestry program is now in place to rehabilitate and replant mangroves in tracts of intertidal wastelands (Ratanasermpong et al. 2000). For this reason, most mangrove stands in the bay are \( \leq 15 \) years old. Fig. 1 Location map of mangrove forests in Sawi Bay (Ao Sawi), and the bay in relation to the southern coast of Thailand (shaded areas mangrove forests; dotted areas intertidal sand flats; S1–S4 study sites) ![Location map of mangrove forests in Sawi Bay (Ao Sawi), and the bay in relation to the southern coast of Thailand](page_104_1042_1732_1202.png) Forests S1 and S2 are located on opposite sides of Khlong Sawi, a small tidal river in the southern part of the bay. Station S1 (10°16.8′N; 99°9.8′E) is a mid-intertidal Rhizophora apiculata forest partially clear-felled 15 years ago, and allowed to regenerate naturally with Avicennia alba as a sub-dominant canopy. The mature trees in this stand are ~25 years old. Above- and below-ground biomass and net canopy primary production are greatest at this site (Table 1). Tidal inundation frequency is ~50% on a monthly average (Wattayakorn et al. 2000). Station S2 (10°16.7′N; 99°9.8′E) is a high-intertidal R. apiculata plantation, manually planted 5 years ago and maintained by the Royal Forestry Dept., Thailand. Above-ground forest biomass and net canopy primary production are lowest at this station (Table 1). The canopy is more open than at station S1, to the extent that ~75% of the forest floor was colonised by a mixture of cyanobacterial mats, as well as green and red macroalgal mats, in the dry season. This site is covered by tides ~10% month⁻¹. Stations S3 (10°22.4′N; 99°13.2′E) and S4 (10°22.4′N; 99°13.3′E) adjoin within the same plantation located in a small tidal estuary, Khlong I Laet, in the northern part of Sawi Bay. This plantation was originally the site of a failed shrimp farm, and was manually replanted 3 years ago. Station S3 is a R. apiculata stand within the mid-intertidal zone, with sediments consisting mostly of silt and clay mixed with very fine sand (Table 1). This site is covered by tides ~25% month⁻¹. Station S4 is located in the high-intertidal zone, and is colonised by Ceriops decandra. Sediment is very fine sand, with equal amounts of silt and clay (Table 1). This site is covered by tides ~10% month⁻¹. Surface water salinity in Khlong Sawi ranged from 8° to 10° in April 1999 and from 1° to 2° in October 1999; freshwater discharge averaged 330,000 and 900,000 m³ day⁻¹ in April and October, respectively (Wattayakorn et. al. 2000). In Khlong I Laet, salinity varied from 20° to 21° during April and from 11° to 12° during October, with freshwater discharge averaging 200,000 and 590,000 m³ day⁻¹ in the dry and wet seasons, respectively (Ayukai et al. 2000). Sediment nitrogen pools, leaf stoichiometry and rainwater Concentrations of free and exchangeable NH₄⁺, as well as NO₂⁻ + NO₃⁻, were determined in both seasons from three cores taken at each site to a depth of 20 cm. Each core was cut at 2-cm intervals in a N₂-filled glove bag. The slices were placed directly into Teflon porewater extractor cassettes (Robbins and Gustinis 1976) containing 0.4 μm Nuclepore filters, and squeezed under N₂ to extract ~10 ml porewater sample⁻¹. Porewater samples for NH₄⁺ (free) and NO₂⁻ + NO₃⁻ were kept frozen until analysis by standard automated techniques (Ryle et al. 1981; Ryle and Wellington 1982). Exchangeable ammonium was determined on a separate set of sediment slices squeezed for porewater using the KCl extraction procedure of Rosenfeld (1979). Sediment total nitrogen content was determined cores (80 to 100 cm length) taken at each site using a 1.5 m stainless steel corer. Each core was sliced at 2- to 5-cm intervals. Sediment slices were squeezed for dissolved nitrogen as detailed above, dried, ground to a powder and analysed for total carbon and total nitrogen on a Perkin Elmer 2400 CHNS/O Series II Analyser. Green leaves were collected from several trees at each site. The leaves were washed in distilled water, dried to constant weight, ground to a powder and analysed for carbon and nitrogen content on a Perkin Elmer 2400 CHNS/O Series II Analyser. Rainwater was collected during both seasons at the field station using a sterile bottle mounted on a retort stand placed atop a 25 cm high plastic container. The rainwater was filtered (0.45 μm Minisart filter) using a sterile syringe, and frozen until analysis. Dissolved nitrogen fluxes Fluxes of NH₄⁺ (NO₂⁻ + NO₃⁻) and dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) across the sediment–water interface were made from three clear and three opaque glass chambers (surface area = 0.007 m²) inserted into boxcorer samples and incubated in a shaded water bath at ambient temperature (Alongi et al. 2001). Each boxcore liner was inserted into the forest floor at each site to a depth of 25 cm and removed with minimal disturbance. Each chamber had an electric-motor propeller unit and a sampling port from which samples for nutrients were taken at 30-min intervals for 3 h. Samples were filtered (0.45 μm Minisart filters and sterile plastic syringe) and processed by automated analysis. DON concentrations were determined by the difference in samples measured for total dissolved nitrogen before and after 12 h photo-oxidation. Net ammonification Net ammonium production was estimated using a core incubation method (Alongi et al. 2001). Two sets of duplicate cores (20 cm length, 7 cm i.d.) were placed in a N₂-filled glove bag and sliced into 4-cm intervals. Each set of duplicate slices was placed in an airtight opaque plastic box. For each depth, there were two boxes each containing duplicate slices, resulting in a total of ten boxes per site. Large roots were removed, and sediments and fine roots mixed in a positive-pressure N₂ atmosphere. Each box was sub-sampled on day 0 and on either day 1 or day 2. Each of two sub-samples per box was mixed with 5–10 ml 1 M KCl solution. They were allowed to stand for 1 h, then placed in the same porewater extractor cassettes used in the porewater analyses (see above) and squeezed under N₂ to obtain ~10 ml porewater which was analysed for ammonium (Ryle et al. 1981; Ryle and Wellington 1982). The changes in ammonium concentration (corrected for KCl dilution) were regressed with time to derive a net ammonification rate. Nitrification The rate of nitrification was estimated using the acetylene inhibition technique (Sloth et al. 1992). In this method, six opaque chambers (the same chambers used for solute fluxes) per site were inserted to a known depth (usually 5 cm) into the forest floor, removed with daily net canopy production rates of Alongi and Dixon (2000) were corrected for night-time canopy respiration using the empirical data of Clough et al. The chambers were then incubated in a flowing ambient water bath, and measured for sediment–water fluxes of ammonium, before and after inhibition of nitrification with acetylene. The difference in the slope of ammonium versus time between the treatments corresponded to the rate of nitrification, assuming that acetylene does not affect other transformation processes (Sloth et al. 1992). Denitrification Denitrification was measured from replicate cores taken from each site using the N2-gas flux technique of Nowicki (1994). Sediment cores (volume range: 230–385 cm3; sediment depth range: 6–10 cm) were taken by pushing open-ended plastic bottles into the sediment surface. Each core was placed into a gas-tight glass chamber (23.5 cm height, 7.6 cm i.d.). The sediment in each chamber was covered with ~500 to 800 ml of creek water sparged with either an 80% He/20% O2 mixture (experimental chambers) or 100% He (control chambers) to remove N2, and, in the case of the experimental cores, to maintain air-saturated O2 concentrations. The overlying water in each sealed chamber was stirred continuously. All chambers were incubated for 9 days in the dark at ambient temperatures to mimic field conditions as closely as possible. The water overlying sediments was replaced every 1–2 days with low-N2 seawater, and the gas phase in the experimental chambers (four per site) was flushed repeatedly with an 80% He/20% O2 mixture. The water exchanges maintained O2 conditions and an adequate nitrate supply. The control chambers (two per site) were incubated under anaerobic conditions (100% He gas and deoxygenated water exchanges) in order to block nitrification and denitrification (Nowicki 1994). Water exchange in all chambers was carried out on day 3, followed by a 3–5 min gas flush immediately after and again 8 h after the water exchange. After day 3, each chamber was sealed and gas samples were withdrawn for measurement of N2 and O2 concentrations in the headspace. The accumulation of N2 gas in the headspace was measured each day for the next 5 days. A He-flushed syringe was used to sample headspace gas. The gas was analysed for N2 and O2 using an MTI Analytical Instruments P200 gas chromatograph under conditions as specified by Nowicki (1994). Calibration standards were run with each set of samples using a certified gas mixture (3% N2, 20% O2, 77% He). Although denitrification was blocked in the control cores, there can be significant de-gassing of N2 diffusing from the sediment porewater to the overlying water and gas. This background flux of N2 (Fdg) was subtracted from the total N2 flux (Ft) to derive the rate of N2 flux due to denitrification (Fdn), where Fdn = Ft - Fdg (Nowicki 1994). Denitrification rates were calculated as the average rate from the replicate cores from each site, from three to four individual incubation periods. Nitrogen fixation Nitrogen fixation in sediments and fine roots at each site was measured in three clear and two dark glass chambers using the acetylene reduction technique (Capone 1993). Sediments and fine roots were obtained by inserting the open-ended chambers (surface area: 64 cm2) into the forest floor to a depth of 10 cm. The chambers were then gently withdrawn from the sediment with minimal disturbance by cutting large roots and sediments at the bottom of each chamber. The chamber bottom was then sealed with a plastic lid lined with soft rubber. After return to the laboratory, the chambers were sealed at the top with a self-contained, battery propeller unit to stir the gas overlying the sediment and roots. A side port was sealed with rubber of low gas permeability to equalise gas pressure. A second side port was sealed with a rubber stopper through which gas samples were taken and acetylene was added to the chamber headspace. Acetylene was added to each chamber to a final volume of from 10% to 15% of the total gas space. After stirring for 15 min, gas samples were taken immediately and then hourly for 3 h, with a final sampling at ~20 h. Acetylene and ethylene were analysed simultaneously by gas chromatography using standards of 5% acetylene and 0.5% ethylene. The acetylene reduction rates were converted to rates of nitrogen fixation using the theoretical factor of three acetylene molecules equalling one nitrogen molecule. Data analysis Differences in parameters were tested using either two-way (site×depth and site×time) or three-way (site×depth×time) ANOVA followed by Ryan’s Q-test (Day and Quinn 1989) for multiple comparisons. Linear regression analysis was used to explore relationships between variables. Linear regression analysis was used to estimate flux rates of gases and solutes by regressing concentrations with time. A significance level of \( P = 0.05 \) was accepted. Results Sediment nitrogen pools Interstitial ammonium and nitrite and nitrate concentrations were so highly variable that there were few significant differences among the four sites with season. At forest sites S1, S3 and S4 concentrations of porewater ammonium during the SW monsoon season were, on average, twice the NE monsoon concentrations (Table 2), but not statistically different. Variations with increasing sediment depth were large, with no significant increasing or decreasing depth patterns (data not shown). Between-core variability was > 100% of the mean at all depth intervals for most sites. At sites S1 and S2, exchangeable ammonium concentrations were two to three times greater than free ammonium. Nitrite and nitrate concentrations were measurable down-core at all sites (Table 2) and were significantly greater during the NE monsoon at forest sites S1 and S4. With the exception of sites S3 and S4 during the NE monsoon, overlying water-column concentrations were greater than in the porewater. Mean concentrations of solid-phase total nitrogen (Table 2) were not significantly different between seasons. There were, however, differences among forests in the following order: S3 > S4 > S1 > S2 (both seasons; differences between S4 and S1 and between S1 and S2 were not significantly different). There were large inter-core variations in total N concentrations with sediment depth, but there no clear increasing or decreasing trends down-core. Sediment–water solute exchange Most (13 of 16) ammonium fluxes were into the sediment (Table 3). Seasonal differences were significant only at S1 and S2, with greater fluxes during the NE monsoon. Differences between ammonium fluxes in clear and darkened chambers were significant only at S2 and S3, where fluxes were in opposite directions during the SW monsoon and NE monsoon, respectively. All of the \( \mathrm{NO}_2^- + \mathrm{NO}_3^- \) fluxes were into the sediment (Table 3). Fluxes were more rapid in both light and dark chambers at stations S2 and S4 than at S1 and S3 during both seasons (Table 3). Most DON fluxes were into the sediment, with no significant patterns among sites and seasons. Nitrification, denitrification and nitrogen fixation Rates of nitrification (Table 4) were significantly greater during the dry NE monsoon at sites S2, S3 and S4. Rates of nitrification in April differed as follows: S3 > S2 > S4 > S1 (no significant differences between S2, S4 and S1). Nitrification in the wet season was measurable only at S1 and S3 (Table 4). Denitrification (Table 5) was measurable only at S4 during the NE monsoon. During the SW monsoon season, denitrification rates were not significantly different among the four mangrove stands. Rates of nitrogen fixation (Table 6) were not significantly different between light and dark chambers at any site during either season. There was no measurable nitrogen fixation at S1. Seasonal and site differences were not significant, as rates were very variable among replicate chambers. Net ammonification Net ammonium production rates (Table 7) ranged from 490 to 2260 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) among the four forests during the NE monsoon, and from 280 to 1505 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) during the SW monsoon. Rates of net ammonification were significantly greater during the NE monsoon at S3 and S4, and during the SW monsoon at S1. Site differences in rates of net ammonification were: S3 > S2 > S1 > S4 (NE monsoon; difference not significant between S1 and S4) and S2 > S3 > S1 > S4 (SW monsoon; difference not significant between S3 and S1).

 860 Data on sediment mass accumulation rates derived from 210Pb (Table 1, Alongi et al. 2001) coupled with the nitrogen flows allowed construction of preliminary nitrogen budgets for all four forests (Table 9). Estimates of nitrogen burial were calculated by multiplying the mass accumulation rates (Table 1) by the mean sediment total nitrogen concentrations (average of both seasons, Table 2). The process measurements averaged for each season were used to estimate total nitrogen input, the percentage burial of the total nitrogen input, and the percentage of total nitrogen flowing through the ammonium pool. Total nitrogen input was estimated as the sum of gross ammonification/root-associated nitrogen fixation (i.e. mangrove nitrogen demand), solute flux, precipitation, burial and surface nitrogen fixation, assuming total input must equal total outputs plus accumulation. Groundwater inputs were not measured. Total nitrogen inputs ranged from 11 to 37 mmol N m−2 day−1 (Table 9), with the highest input in the oldest forest and the lowest inputs at the two forests receiving the least tidal inundation (S2 and S4). The bulk of the nitrogen flow (68–88%) was through the ammonium pool via ammonification/root-associated nitrogen fixation, with comparatively slow fluxes across the air/water–sediment interface. Nitrogen fixation and precipitation were smaller inputs than uptake from overlying tidal water (Table 9). The precipitation inputs were derived by multiplying annual rainfall (1,800 mm; Wattayakorn et al. 2000) by mean concentrations of rainwater NH4+ (2.5 μM) and NO2− + NO3− (0.9 μM). Denitrification was a small loss in relation to nitrogen loading at sites S1–S3 (3–6%), but a much greater percentage loss at the Ceriops forest (23%). A total of 4–12% of nitrogen input was buried, with the greatest burial at the less frequently inundated forests S2 and S4. Discussion Our data indicate a high demand for below-ground nitrogen in order to sustain the rapid rates of net canopy production measured in the Sawi Bay mangrove forests. Nitrogen cycling below the forest floor must be regulated, not only by rates and pathways of nitrogen input and transformation, but also by rates of tree uptake. Forests located lower in the seascape (sites S1 and S3) were inundated more often than the other two forests located higher in the tidal zone, processed more nitrogen through the ammonium pool, and received greater import of particulate and dissolved nitrogen from the sea. Conversely, the sediments of less tidally inundated forests were exposed to the atmosphere for longer time periods. The oldest forest (site S1) – where the most rapid rates of canopy photosynthesis and rates of nitrogen input were measured – was inundated by tides more often than the other stands. The forests located at the greatest tidal height (sites S2 and S4) were functionally similar, in that both stands had the slowest rates of canopy production, received the lowest rates of nitrogen input, and shunted the least amount of nitrogen through the interstitial ammonium pools. Of these two stands, the younger Ceriops forest lost proportionally more nitrogen via denitrification than the other stands. The higher rates of denitrification at site S4 can be attributed to generally higher concentrations of porewater nitrate (Table 2), as the availability of nitrate is an important factor controlling denitrification rates in aquatic sediments (Seitzinger 1988). The higher nitrate concentrations in S4 sediments may be the result of chemical oxidation of ammonium due to the frequent exposure to the atmosphere and rainwater; biological factors are less likely, considering that nitrification rates were not greater at this location than in the other three forests. The more rapid microbial transformations in sediments of forests more seaward can most likely be attributed to more frequent wetting and deposition of materials from tidal water. Sediments of the higher intertidal forests were frequently dry for prolonged periods or subject to percolation of rainwater; such oscillations in wetness and salinity may slow rates of microbial activity. Earlier mangrove studies noted lower bacterial abundance and activity in high intertidal sediments (Alongi 1987; Kristensen et al. 1995) that were attributed to coarser sediments, less organic matter and lower moisture than mangrove deposits located more seaward. At the Sawi Bay sites, there were no clear differences in sediment organic carbon and nitrogen content between either the low (S1 and S3) or the high intertidal (S2 and S4) sites. However, sediments at sites S1 and S3 were finer, with significantly more silt and clay, and lower redox potential (Alongi et al. 2001). Our nitrogen budgets are preliminary, averaging seasonal data, so they do not reflect processes that were either not measured (e.g. dissimilatory nitrate reduction, groundwater) or were likely operating on smaller spatial or temporal scales. For instance, the algal mats of forest site S2 were very productive (15 mmol C m^{-2} day^{-1}; Alongi et al. 2001) and based on an average C:N ratio of 14, required 1,055 μmol N m^{-2} day^{-1}. It is possible that a substantial proportion of denitrification and DON uptake from overlying tidal waters was taking place within these mats. Microbial mats cycle nitrogen rapidly, much of which is internally recycled as a closed system (Paerl and Pinkney 1996). The reliability of our mass balance estimates depends on the accuracy of our net canopy primary production measurements and the validity of our notion that ammonification and/or root-associated N2 fixation in sub-surface sediments is the main source of nitrogen supporting tree growth. Net daytime photosynthetic production (PN) was calculated from empirical measurements of the leaf area index (L, Alongi and Dixon 2000) and the average rate of photosynthesis (Ac, Clough et al. 2000a) such that \( P_N = d \times L \times A_c \) (Clough et al. 2000b), where \( d \) is daylength. These estimates were corrected by subtracting empirical measurements of night-time respiration (Clough et al. 2000a), which, on average, equalled 31% of \( P_N \). Net canopy production measured in this way results in productivity rates several times greater than previous estimates for mangroves (Bunt et al. 1979) using methods that are now known to be insufficient to account for observed accumulation of above-ground biomass (Clough 1992). Our assumption that tree production is supported mainly via the ammonium pool by ammonification and/or nitrogen fixation in deep sediments is tenable, given that most other inputs were measured and found to be small. Incorporation of particulate nitrogen into the forest floor via litterfall and other processes (e.g. crab burial) would be accounted for in the mass accumulation measurements using \( ^{210}\mathrm{Pb} \) (Table 1). Translocation of nitrogen within the trees was not measured, but is likely to be within the maximum range of 5–15% based on differences in nitrogen content between green and senescent leaves, and litterfall measured in other Rhizophora forests (Li et al. 1999). Mass balances of nitrogen in other mangrove ecosystems have pointed to the importance of ammonium uptake in mangrove nutrition (Kristensen et al. 1995; Alongi 1998). Most nitrogen required to sustain net production in mixed Rhizophora forests in northern Australia is derived from the ammonium pool via ammonification, with much less flow via the nitrate pool by nitrification, or by nitrogen fixation. In Thai forests at Ao Nam Bor, Kristensen et al. (1995) similarly found that nearly all of the nitrogen required for low- and mid-intertidal R. apiculata forests was derived from below-ground mineralisation processes. Internal recycling mechanisms such as turnover of microbes and fine roots were not measured. However, the imbalance between the dissolved inorganic nitrogen fluxes across the sediment–water interface and the net production of ammonium in the sediment indicate either some methodological shortcomings or net uptake of ammonium by the trees and microbes during sediment incubation. Furthermore, the incubation method used to measure ammonification does not fully account for sorption reactions or reactions between ammonium and other solutes. Our rates are within the range of those measured by Kristensen et al. (2000) using a similar method in mangroves further south of Sawi Bay. Kristensen et al. (2000) also observed an imbalance between rates of ammonium production and sediment–water exchange, and attributed it to rapid and efficient assimilation by sediment microbes, rather than to uptake by fine mangrove roots. Uptake by roots is likely, but microbial uptake cannot be discounted, given the high C:N ratio of mangrove organic matter – significantly higher than the need by heterotrophic bacteria for organic substrates with a C:N ratio of \( \leq 10 \) (Fenchel et al. 1998). Mangroves may supplement their nitrogen requirements from algal nitrogen fixation on prop roots and stems (Alongi 1996), but little, if any, significant algal flora was observed on the trees in Sawi Bay. Therefore, in order to meet the measured rates of net canopy production, either significant nitrogen fixation and/or ammonification must be occurring within roots and rhizomes in deeper sediments. We did not take any measurements below 5–20 cm depth, but other studies in similar forests have detected microbial communities actively growing up to 1 m deep in the sediment (Alongi 1987). Active nitrogen fixation in roots and rhizomes in deep sediment layers is known (Zuberer and Silver 1978; Holgiun et al. 1992). Our estimates of nitrogen fixation were made with shallow sediment cores containing fine roots and pieces of large excised roots, and may be underestimates. Measurements of ammonification in deep vegetated sediments are problematical due to rapid uptake and turnover between interstitial ammonium and organisms and to exchange between free and fixed ammonium pools. Arguably the most accurate measurements of ammonification in mangrove sediments have been made using \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) in surface sediments in other Rhizophora forests in Thailand (Blackburn et al. 1987; Kristensen et al. 1995, 1998) and in Jamaica (Nedwell et al. 1994). Extrapolating the data from these studies to a sediment depth of 1 m, our estimate of a large flux via the ammonium pool to trees is credible, and could conceivably be sustained by ammonification. Our estimates of ammonium turnover (Table 9) on the order of a few hours to 2 days agree with the turnover times calculated by Nedwell et al. (1994) in the Jamaican forests. Our mass balance estimates require high rates of nitrogen input (11–37 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) into these forests (Table 9). Most particulate nitrogen imported by these stands likely originates from upstream rather than downstream sources (Ayukai et al. 2000; Alongi et al. 2001). Radiochemical data on mass sediment accumulation rates show a high \( ^{137}\mathrm{Cs} \) inventory in these sediments (Table 1) compared with estimated rates of atmospheric input (Alongi et al. 2001). As caesium is very soluble in seawater, it is likely that the high inventory reflects Cs that has not been in contact with seawater for a substantial period of time. This interpretation is reasonable, because the waterways discharging into Sawi Bay have experienced large increases in organic load due to an increase in the number of sewage outlets, abandonment of a large number of shrimp ponds and erosion from increased land clearing for agriculture (Ratanasermpong et al. 2000). The low burial and rapid mineralisation rates imply that the quality of organic matter deposited at the floor of the forests was high. A study of the dynamics of dissolved and particulate nutrients in the mangrove creeks of Sawi Bay found low elemental C:N (3–5:1) and N:P (2–3:1) ratios of particles in creek waters (Ayukai et al. 2000). These low stoichiometric ratios imply high-quality organic matter in the creeks. Ayukai et al. (2000) attributed this quality to the labile composition of effluent from shrimp ponds, where nitrogen-enriched feeds are used for enhancing shrimp production; to sewage being discharged from adjacent catchments; and to enhanced growth and abundance of phytoplankton. The budget estimates of nitrogen for these forests – coupled with the mass balance of nitrogen for Sawi Bay (Wattayakorn et al. 2000) – imply that most nitrogen is depositing within the forests and accumulating in tree biomass. Most of the forests lining the bay are young and actively growing, with most stands \( \leq 15 \) years old. Nitrogen retention has similarly been suggested for other tropical mangrove forests (Nedwell et al. 1994; Rivera-Monroy and Twilley 1996). Numerous processes and mechanisms have been offered to explain nitrogen retention, including rapid deposition of particulate nitrogen (Morell and Corredor 1993), leaf resorption and translocation (Rao et al. 1994), inhibition of denitrification by anoxic metabolites (Rivera-Monroy et al. 1995), dissimilatory reduction of nitrate to ammonium (Rivera-Monroy and Twilley 1996), and microbial exudation of proteinaceous materials and/or accumulation by bacteria and fungi on particles (Rivera-Monroy and Twilley 1996). Aber (1992) suggests that, in nitrogen-limited terrestrial forests, most nitrogen uptake by trees and microbes is in the form of ammonium, as nitrification is inhibited by competition with trees, microflora and other decomposers. Immobilisation of nitrate may be driven by large dissolved organic carbon (DOC) pools produced during decomposition of low-nitrogen plant litter, and by root exudation. Mangrove forests have similarly large pools of DOC, fuelled by below-ground decomposition of litter. Thus, our data indicate that extensive uptake of ammonium by the trees and microbes is associated with slow rates of nitrification. Also, like other forests, a large fraction of the total detrital pool in mangroves is in the form of wood that decays slowly (Robertson and Daniel 1989), acting as a long-term source of nutrients and a site for nitrogen fixation and possibly denitrification (Boto and Robertson 1990). It appears that the behaviour and cycling of nitrogen in mangrove forests may be more functionally similar to other forests than to their supposed salt marsh counterparts. Aller for insightful comments on an earlier draft. This is contribution no. 1090 from the Australian Institute of Marine Science.

G. Wattayakorn · B.F. Clough

Below-ground nitrogen cycling in relation to net canopy production in mangrove forests of southern Thailand

Received: 14 June 2001 / Accepted: 1 November 2001 / Published online: 18 January 2002
© Springer-Verlag 2002

Abstract Rates of accumulation, transformation and availability of sediment nitrogen in four mangrove forests of different age and type in southern Thailand were examined in relation to forest net canopy production. Net ammonification (range: 0.3–2.3 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)), nitrification (range: 0–0.7 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) and nitrogen fixation (range: 0–0.6 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) in surface sediments equated to <10% of canopy nitrogen demand (range: 7.5–32 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)). By mass balance, we estimated that most of the nitrogen required for tree growth must be derived from root-associated nitrogen fixation and/or mineralisation processes occurring possibly to the maximum depth of live root penetration (75–100 cm). Denitrification, nitrification, rainfall and tidal exchange were comparatively small components of sediment nitrogen flow. Denitrification (range: 0–3.8 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) removed 3–6% of total nitrogen input at three Rhizophora forests, but removed 23% of total nitrogen input in a high-intertidal Ceriops forest. Nitrogen burial ranged from 4% to 12% of total nitrogen input, with the greatest burial rates in two forests receiving the least tidal inundation. Inputs of nitrogen to the forests were rapid (range: 11–37 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)), likely originating from upstream sources such as agricultural and industrial lands, sewage and shrimp ponds. Our results indicate that ~70% to 90% of the nitrogen supplied to the forest floor is shunted via the ammonium pool to trees to sustain the rapid rates of net canopy production measured in these forests. Differences in plant–sediment nitrogen relations between the forests appeared to be a function of the interaction between intertidal position and stand age.

Introduction

Most mangrove forests are either nitrogen or phosphorus limited (Alongi 1998). Fertilisation experiments (Boto and Wellington 1983; Boto et al. 1985), and the fact that mangroves appear to be highly efficient in retaining and recycling nutrients (Nedwell et al. 1994; Kristensen et al. 1995), support the notion of nutrient limitation.

The pathways of nutrient cycling in mangrove forests are poorly understood. Nutrient availability and use are thought to depend upon several interrelated factors: the sources and composition of labile organic matter, inorganic nutrient pools, frequency of tidal flooding, temperature, salinity, soil chemistry, tree physiology and solar radiation (Ball 1988; Alongi 1998). For instance, a large fraction of interstitial ammonium is bound to soil particles and exchangeable with other cations. The kinetics of ion exchange between the free and exchangeable ammonium pools in saline soils is, however, very complex and dynamic. The availability of nitrogen in forms capable of being readily assimilated by mangroves is a microbial controlled process, with the bacterial breakdown of organic nitrogen as the major rate-limiting step.

Knowledge of nitrogen transformation in mangrove sediments is limited. Individual processes such as denitrification and nitrogen fixation have been measured in a number of mangrove forests (Nedwell et al. 1994; Rivera-Monroy and Twilley 1996; Kristensen et al. 1998). Ammonification has been measured, but most methods cannot distinguish gross and net (after biological uptake) production rates. The Mekong River plume fuels nitrogen fixation and determines phytoplankton species distribution in the South China Sea during low- and high-discharge season Julia Grossea,1,* Deniz Bombar,a Hai Nhu Doan,b Lam Ngoc Nguyen,b and Maren Vossa a Leibnitz Institute for Baltic Sea Research, Department of Biology, Warnemuende, Germany b Institute of Oceanography Nha Trang, Nha Trang, Vietnam Abstract The influence of the Mekong River (South China Sea) on N2 fixation and phytoplankton distribution was investigated during the lowest- and highest-discharge seasons (April 2007 and September 2008, respectively). The river plays an essential role in providing nutrients (nitrate, phosphate, silicate) for the adjacent sea and creates different salinity and nutrient gradients over different seasons. River water (salinity 0), mesohaline waters (salinity 14–32), a transition zone with salinities between 32 and 33.5, and marine waters (salinity above 33.5) were sampled at different spatial resolutions in both cruises. High N2 fixation rates were measured during both seasons, with rates of up to 5.05 nmol N L−1 h−1 in surface waters under nitrogen-replete conditions, increasing to 22.77 nmol N L−1 h−1 in nitrogen-limited waters. Asymbiotic diatoms were found only close to the river mouth, and symbiotic diatoms, which potentially hosted diazotrophs, were most abundant in waters where N2 fixation rates were highest, nitrate concentrations were at the detection limit, and phosphate and silicate were still available. Filamentous cyanobacteria like Trichodesmium were present only in marine waters with salinities above 33.5. Overall, N2 fixation accounts for 1–47% of the nitrogen demand of primary production. Dinitrogen (N2) fixation plays an important role in fueling the oligotrophic ocean with nitrogen (N) (Mulholland 2007). Recent studies propose that N2 fixation may also be significant in coastal and other nutrient rich environments (Deutsch et al. 2007; Bonnet et al. 2009). In this context, river plumes have been suggested to host other groups of N2-fixing organisms than the typical open-ocean diazotrophs Trichodesmium and unicellular cyanobacteria (Capone et al. 1997; Church et al. 2005a); for example, in the Amazon River plume, diatom–diazotroph associations (DDAs) can displace Trichodesmium as the dominant diazotroph of the region, and rates of N2 fixation in DDA blooms exceed vertical nitrate fluxes (Carpenter et al. 1999; Subramaniam et al. 2008). Diatoms hosting diazotroph symbionts come from various genera. Hemiaulus, Rhizosolenia, Guinardia, and Bacteriastrum associate with the heterocystous cyanobacterium Richelia intracellularis, while diatoms of the genus Chaetoceros are typically found in symbiosis with Calothrix rhizosoleniae, another diazotroph cyanobacterium that is closely related to Richelia (Carpenter 2002; Foster and Zehr 2006). The trichomes of Richelia intracellularis reside as an endosymbiont between the plasmalemma and the frustule of the diatom in Hemiaulus, Rhizosolenia, and Guinardia (Villareal 1992). In the DDAs Bacteriastrum-Richelia intracellularis and Chaetoceros-Calothrix rhizosoleniae, the symbiont resides as an epiphyte on the spines of the diatom (Carpenter 2002; Foster and O’Mullan 2008). Studies by Foster and others (2007) later confirmed that DDAs (Hemiaulus-Richelia) dominate in the Amazon River plume waters with measurable concentrations of nitrate (NO3−) (< 0.01–0.13 μmol L−1), phosphate (PO4−3) (< 0.02–0.13 μmol L−1), and silicate (Si[OH]4−) (0.3–11.3 μmol L−1), while Trichodesmium and different groups of free-living unicellular cyanobacteria were more abundant in oceanic waters outside the river plume, where nutrients were below the detection limit (Foster et al. 2007; Subramaniam et al. 2008). Also in the Congo River plume in the Eastern Equatorial Atlantic, conditions seem to be favorable for DDAs, even though Trichodesmium dominated the diazotroph community (Foster et al. 2008). The DDAs are thought to have a growth advantage in river plumes where nitrogen is limiting but phosphorus and silicate are still available, while nitrogen is supplied through N2 fixation by the diazotroph symbiont (Janson et al. 1999; Carpenter 2002). Furthermore, tropical rivers provide trace metals such as iron (Nittrouer et al. 1995; Bergquist and Boyle 2006), which is an essential component of the dinitrogenase enzyme complex of all diazotrophs. All these findings suggest that enhanced N2 fixation in tropical river plumes might be a global phenomenon and would thus contribute substantially to oceanic N2 fixation. Like other tropical rivers, the Mekong River discharges relatively high concentrations of nutrients, with over 40 μmol L−1 of nitrate plus nitrite (NO3−+NO2−) and about 1 μmol L−1 of PO4−3 and over 100 μmol Si(OH)4− (http://www.gemstat.org). These nutrients foster new production in the South China Sea (SCS), into which the Mekong River discharges. Previous results from the SCS show that the Mekong River plume is linked to elevated rates of N2 fixation as far as 200 km northeast of the river mouth (Voss et al. 2006), which suggests a scenario similar to the one in the Amazon River plume. The study by Voss et al. (2006) investigated the Vietnamese upwelling area and the adjacent offshore oligotrophic region, where diazotroph species were possibly influenced by both riverine and initially upwelled nutrients. In contrast to the study by Voss et al. (2006), we carried out a detailed sampling closer to the river mouth, where the changes in salinity and nutrient concentrations are expected to have the greatest influence on species composition and rates of \( N_2 \) fixation. The diazotroph community in the SCS includes DDAs, *Trichodesmium*, and unicellular diazotrophs (\(< 10 \ \mu m\)), comprising coccoid cyanobacteria and proteobacteria (Moisander et al. 2008), and it can be expected that the Mekong River plume triggers unequal distribution patterns of these different groups. In the present study, we measured rates of \( N_2 \) fixation and determined phytoplankton species composition in SCS surface waters off the Mekong river mouth. The study compares two field investigations, one conducted in April 2007, coinciding with intermonsoon and the river’s lowest annual outflow, and a second investigation conducted in September 2008 during southwest (SW) monsoon and the river’s highest annual outflow (Hoa et al. 2007). The goals of this study are to describe and compare the biogeochemical settings of the river plume during both seasons and to assess how these settings are related to \( N_2 \) fixation and to the distribution of phytoplankton, including asymbiotic diatoms, *Trichodesmium* spp., and different diatom species that potentially host diazotroph symbionts. Methods *Study area*—The Mekong Delta lies between 9.0°N and 10.5°N in the Southeast Asian monsoon region. The SW monsoon between June and September coincides with the rainy season and the rivers largest annual outflow (40,000 m³ s⁻¹; Hoa et al. 2007). During this time of the year, the winds have an approximate speed of 6 m s⁻¹ (Hellerman and Rosenstein 1983) and deflect the river plume northeast along the coast before it turns east into the open SCS. The northeast (NE) monsoon appears between November and March, coinciding with the dry season, and the prevailing winds have an average velocity of 9 m s⁻¹ (Hellerman and Rosenstein 1983). The intermonsoon during April and May and during October and early November marks the transition between monsoon seasons (Fang et al. 2002). In April, at the end of the dry season, the river outflow reaches its annual low with an outflow of about 2100 m³ s⁻¹ (Hoa et al. 2007), resulting in a relatively small river plume (covering approximately 37,000 km² of the SCS), which is deflected southward. The total freshwater discharge of the Mekong River is about 500 km³ yr⁻¹, with 15% being discharged during the dry season and 85% during the rainy season (Hoa et al. 2007). Compared to the Amazon and Congo Rivers with 6900 and 1300 km³ yr⁻¹, respectively (Korzun 1978; World Hydrology Cycle Observing System, http://www.whycos.org), the discharge by the Mekong River is low, but it is the largest river draining into the SCS. Annual loads of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) are modeled for the river mouth reaching \( 2.7 \times 10^4 \) t TN yr⁻¹ and \( 9.0 \times 10^2 \) t TP yr⁻¹ (Yoshimura and Takeuschi 2007). The model also predicts a discharge of 0.1 kg TN s⁻¹ during the dry season (December through May) and 10 kg TN s⁻¹ during the rainy season (May through November) (Yoshimura and Takeuschi 2007). *Sampling*—Samples were collected aboard a Vietnamese monitoring vessel, BTh-0666 KN, between 15 April and 20 April 2007 (Fig. 1A) and between 18 September and 22 September 2008 (Fig. 1B). About 40% of the total water volume is discharged from the southernmost river arm (Sta. 3 in April 2007 and Sta. 24 in September 2008), whereas the other river arms represented by Sta. 20 and Sta. 2 (April 2007) and Sta. 1 and Sta. 12 (September 2008) discharge ~ 30% and 13%, respectively (Nguyen et al. 2008). Northeasterly winds of 10 to 12 m s⁻¹ occurred during a 2-week period before the cruise in April 2007 and mixed the entire water column. Throughout the first 4 d of the cruise in April 2007 (Sta. 1–20), winds did not restrict sampling, ![Map of the Mekong River Estuary with all CTD stations of (A) April 2007 and (B) September 2008. The map was created with the Surfer® 8.09 (Golden Software).](page_1042_312_768_1012.png) Fig. 1. Map of the Mekong River Estuary with all CTD stations of (A) April 2007 and (B) September 2008. The map was created with the Surfer® 8.09 (Golden Software). but on the northernmost transect (Sta. 21–25), winds of 6 m s\(^{-1}\) allowed sampling only for nutrient concentrations and phytoplankton composition. Three transects were sampled; each started in a river arm and was directed out to the open sea. We planned to sample the same stations in September 2008, but because of constant winds between 5 and 10 m s\(^{-1}\), sampling farther offshore was impossible and was kept close to the coast. At all stations, the entire water column was measured for conductivity, temperature and depth (CTD) with Seabird sensors (SEB19 plus), and turbidity with a Seapoint Turbidity Meter (recording Nephelometric Turbidity Units [NTU], waters below 10 NTU have moderate plant and animal life; waters below 1 NTU represent oligotrophic conditions; CWT 2004). A total of 25 (April 2007) and 35 (September 2008) surface samples (0–1 m) were taken with a 10-L Niskin bottle. A 24-h time-series station (Sta. 19; Fig. 1A) was sampled between 05:30 h on 18 April 2007 and 07:00 h on 19 April 2007. The time-series station was sampled hourly with the CTD and provided a total of seven sampling points (SP) for nutrients, chlorophyll, phytoplankton, N\(_2\) fixation, and primary production (sampling every 3 h during the day, every 6 h during the night). The same station (Sta. 28; Fig. 1B) was sampled again between 11:40 h on 20 September 2008 and 11:40 h on 21 September 2008, providing hourly measurements with a CTD between 11:40 h and 17:40 h (20 September 2008) as well as 05:40 h and 11:40 h (21 September 2008) and a total of four SP for chlorophyll, N\(_2\) fixation, primary production, and phytoplankton (sampling every 6 h) as well as six SP for nutrients (sampling every 3 h). The geographical position of this time-series station was chosen in order to enable sampling of the hydrographic situation of the Mekong River plume throughout a complete tidal cycle. Analysis—Water samples for the determination of NO\(_3\), NO\(_2\), PO\(_4\), and Si(OH)\(_4\) were taken, filtered through WHATMAN GF/F glass-fiber filters (0.7-\(\mu\)m pore size), and stored frozen onboard before they were analyzed at the Institute of Oceanography, Nha Trang. Standard colorimetric methods (Grasshoff et al. 1983) were used. These methods usually reach a precision of 0.05 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) for NO\(_3\), 0.01 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) for NO\(_2\), 0.01 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) for PO\(_4\), and 0.1 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) for Si(OH)\(_4\). However, because of the local circumstances (nutrient traces in the only available distilled water), we could not achieve a precision better than 0.05 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) for NO\(_3\), NO\(_2\), and PO\(_4\). Nutrient ratios (N : P, Si : N) were therefore not calculated for samples having unreliable concentrations \(\leq 0.1\) \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\). Chlorophyll \(a\) (Chl \(a\)) was measured at 12 stations in April 2007 and at 15 stations in September 2008. A water volume between 100 and 2000 mL was used to cover a Whatman GF/F glass-fiber filter appropriately with organic material. Chlorophyll samples were stored frozen at \(-80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) until analyzed. Chlorophyll was extracted in ethanol and measured with a Turner 10-AU-005 fluorometer (Wasmund et al. 2006). Samples for phytoplankton identification (1.5 liters) were taken at 21 stations (April 2007) and 13 stations (September 2008) and preserved with 0.5 mL formaldehyde (33%) and 10 mL of Lugol solution, according to the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission protocol (Hallegraeff 1995). Phytoplankton identification and counting by light microscopy included only the size fraction > 10 \(\mu\)m and was carried out using standard protocols after Utermöhl (1958). A fluorescence microscope for the detection of intracellular symbionts was not available. Rates of N\(_2\) fixation and primary production were measured using the tracer assay described by Montoya et al. (1996). Surface water was taken with Niskin bottles at nine stations in April 2007 and at 13 stations in September 2008. The water was filled into three 2.3-liter Nalgene bottles at each station. The Nalgene bottles were equipped with septum caps made of Teflon-lined butyl rubber. Subsequently, both \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\)-gas (2 mL; Sercon, 99 atom%) and 0.1 \(\mu\)mol L\(^{-1}\) NaH\(^{13}\mathrm{CO}_3\) solution (0.5 mL; Sigma Aldrich, 98 atom%) were added with syringes. The bottles were incubated on deck and cooled with surface seawater. During the day, the incubations lasted for 6 h, and the incubators were covered with neutral-density screening (50%), which correspond to the light intensities of surface waters of mesotrophic waters or 10-m depth in oligotrophic waters. At night, the incubations lasted about 12 h to ensure a \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) uptake above the detection limit. Because of the limited cruise time during both investigations, N\(_2\) fixation and primary production incubations were always initiated immediately after sampling so that most day incubations lasted either from 06:00 h to 12:00 h or from 12:00 h to 18:00 h. Incubations during the night covered the entire dark period (Table 1). The incubations were terminated by gentle vacuum filtration. In April 2007, N\(_2\) fixation was measured in two size fractions (< and > 10 \(\mu\)m), and the total N\(_2\) fixation rates were calculated by adding the respective rates. Samples were initially filtered through acid-washed gauze (10-\(\mu\)m pore size). The filamentous cyanobacteria and diatoms (> 10 \(\mu\)m) were then rinsed onto precombusted Whatman GF/F glass-fiber filters (4 h at 500\(^\circ\)C, 0.7-\(\mu\)m pore size). The particles < 10 \(\mu\)m in the filtrate were collected over additional glass-fiber filter. In September 2008 the size fractions were not separated, and only total N\(_2\) fixation rates were measured. All filters were stored frozen at \(-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). In the laboratory, the filters were acidified over fuming hydrochloric acid (37%) for 6 h, subsequently dried (40\(^\circ\)C; 12 h), packed into tin cups, and pelletized. Isotopic measurements of the filters were done with a Delta S (Thermo) isotopic ratio mass spectrometer connected to an elemental analyzer CE1108 via open split interface. Rates of N\(_2\) fixation and primary production were calculated as described by Montoya et al. (1996). The lowest salinity at sampling stations in the River mouth was 14.3 (Sta. 3) and from there, salinities gradually increased to maximal values of around 34 at stations farthest offshore (Fig. 2A). During SW monsoon in September 2008, the outflow was much higher so that freshwater was found in the river arms at Sta. 1 and 24 (Fig. 2B). The plume extended much farther offshore during that cruise; however, because of considerable swell, it was impossible for our small vessel to reach sampling stations as far offshore as in April 2007. Salinities above 30 were measured at outer Sta. 8 and 20, and the maximal salinities were found at Sta. 28, ranging between 31.9 and 32.0. Based on surface salinity and nutrient distributions, we distinguish three station categories, which will be referred to throughout this article: (1) mesohaline (14.3–32.0), which was sampled during both cruises; (2) transitional (> 32.0–33.5); and (3) oceanic (> 33.5), whereby the latter salinities are typical for open sea water as defined by Dippner et al. (2007) for the SCS off Vietnam. Transitional and oceanic salinities were sampled only in April 2007, and, as mentioned, salinities < 14.0 (0.1–8.9) were found only in September 2008. In order to clearly show the differences between the observed salinity gradients during lowest and highest river discharge, the salinity isoline of 32 is highlighted in all figures showing surface distributions. The salinity of 32 was also chosen because it was previously defined as a lower boundary for the occurrence of Trichodesmium (Jones et al. 1982; Revelante and Gilmartin 1982). Overall, concentrations of all nutrients showed a strong offshore gradient and were negatively correlated with salinity in April 2007; in September 2008, only NO3+NO2 and Si(OH)4 showed significantly negative correlations with salinity (Fig. 2C–H; Table 2). The highest concentrations of NO3+NO2, PO4, and Si(OH)4 were encountered within the river arms, at Sta. 2 and 3 in April 2007, and at Sta. 1 in September 2008 (Fig. 2C–H). Interestingly, concentrations of 4.2–19.6 μmol L−1 NO3+NO2 and 0.4–1.0 μmol L−1 PO4 in mesohaline waters in April 2007 did not differ much from concentrations in waters with much lower salinity (≤ 8.9) in September 2008 (17.3–22.3 μmol L−1 NO3+NO2 and 0.6–0.9 μmol L−1 PO4); however, for concentrations of Si(OH)4, there was indeed a clear difference (18.8–42.6 μmol L−1 in mesohaline waters in April 2007 vs. 115–176 μmol L−1 at salinities ≤ 8.9 in September 2008) (Table 3). Mesohaline waters had overall similar nutrient concentrations during both investigations (Table 3). Transitional waters, which were only sampled in April 2007, had NO3+NO2 concentrations of ≤ 0.9 μmol L−1, PO4 of ≤ 0.3 μmol L−1, and Si(OH)4 concentrations of ≤ 10.1 μmol L−1.
